column2: Tecate is a small border city in Baja California located in a valley between Tijuana and Mexicali. The city’s water and wastewater infrastructure is managed by the Comisión Estatal de Servicios Públicos de Tecate (CESPTE).
column3: The city has one municipal wastewater treatment plant that serves the urban area and several nearby communities. Potable water is supplied from local wells and the Rio Tecate.
column4: A NADBank project closure report states that Tecate’s wastewater treatment plant has a capacity of 200 L/s (~4.56 MGD). The project improved the percolation filter but did not increase capacity; effluent now meets BOD and suspended solids standardsnadbank.org/hubfs/proyectos/169_tecate_spa1.pdf#:~:text=capacidad%20para%20200%20l%2Fs
column6: The plant uses percolation and filtration with aerobic processes; upgrades improved effluent quality but capacity remains at 200 L/s. Potable water treatment consists of conventional filtration and chlorination.
column7: Effluent must meet NOM‑001‑ECOL‑1996 for BOD and TSS. Potable water must comply with NOM‑127‑SSA1‑1994.
column8: Wastewater flows vary with tourism and seasonal population changes; effluent quality improved after filter upgrades and now consistently meets BOD and TSS limits.
column9: No quantitative water quality data are publicly available. The report notes that the plant now meets standards for BOD and suspended solidsnadbank.org/hubfs/proyectos/169_tecate_spa1.pdf#:~:text=capacidad%20para%20200%20l%2Fs
column11: Energy use is moderate for aerators and pumps; upgrades focused on improving filtration efficiency.
column12: CESPTE monitors BOD, TSS and bacterial counts; potable water is tested for chlorine residual and coliforms.
column13: Percolation filters and aeration for wastewater; conventional filtration and chlorination for drinking water.
column14: Limited capacity restricts future growth; industrial wastewater may overload the system; groundwater resources are stressed during drought.
column15: Rehabilitating infrastructure, expanding capacity, and exploring water reuse for irrigation could enhance sustainability.
column17: El%20proyecto%20se. Lack of detailed water quality and microplastic data.

column2: Tecate’s small urban watershed drains to the Tecate River and ultimately to the Tijuana River; plastic litter can enter waterways during storm events.
column3: No studies have been published on microplastics in Tecate’s drinking water or wastewater. Given its proximity to Tijuana, similar sources such as road runoff and inadequate waste management likely contribute.
column4: No quantitative data. Regional urban river studies show microplastic concentrations ranging from 0.05–16 particles/m³ (Los Angeles River)ftp.sccwrp.org/pub/download/DOCUMENTS/TechnicalReports/1389_MPLosAngelesSanGabrielRivers.pdf#:~:text=contaminants%20in%20the%20watershed%20may
column7: The wastewater plant does not have advanced filtration designed to remove microplastics. Waste management services and street sweeping help reduce litter.
column8: There are no Mexican regulations for microplastics in water; California’s emerging standards may influence future policy.
column9: No monitoring is available; microplastic loads likely increase during rain events.
column10: Not applicable due to data gaps.
column11: Advanced microplastic removal would increase energy demand; not currently implemented.
column12: Standard microplastic sampling (filtration and FTIR) would be required to establish a baseline.
column13: Potential upgrades include adding tertiary filtration and public campaigns to reduce plastic use.
column14: Lack of data, limited resources, and potential contributions from cross‑border pollution.
column15: Collaboration with universities and cross‑border programs to assess and mitigate microplastics.

column2: Tecate is located in a mountainous region; its groundwater and surface water sources can be affected by industrial effluent and septic discharges.
column3: Contaminants may include BOD, TSS, nutrients, pathogens, and industrial chemicals from local factories. Historically some communities lacked sewer connections, causing untreated sewage to enter the Tecate River.
column4: No numerical contaminant data are publicly available. The NADBank report notes that after upgrades the Tecate wastewater plant meets effluent standards for BOD (monthly average ≤75 mg/L) and TSS (≤75 mg/L)nadbank.org/hubfs/proyectos/169_tecate_spa1.pdf#:~:text=capacidad%20para%20200%20l%2Fs
column6: The upgraded percolation filter improves removal of solids and organic matter. Ongoing maintenance is required to sustain performance.
column7: Effluent standards set by NOM‑001‑ECOL‑1996; potable water standards per NOM‑127‑SSA1‑1994. Industrial dischargers must obtain permits.
column8: Effluent quality has stabilized after upgrades; contamination peaks occur during heavy rains when unsewered areas discharge into the river.
column9: General parameters include BOD, TSS, coliforms and nutrients. Specific measurements are not publicly reported.
column10: Normal operating conditions require aeration and pumping; additional treatment or desalination would increase energy demand.
column11: CESPTE monitors effluent BOD and TSS; limited monitoring for metals or emerging contaminants.
column12: Percolation filters, aeration and chlorination are used; future upgrades could include activated sludge or membrane bioreactors.
column13: Limited capacity to accommodate population growth; contamination from septic systems and industry; lack of funding for advanced treatment.
column14: Expanding sewer coverage, implementing water reuse projects, and seeking cross‑border funding.
column16: El%20proyecto%20se; no quantitative water quality data available.

column2: Tecate’s drinking water comes from local wells and surface sources; distribution is managed by CESPTE.
column3: Water quality information is scarce. High mineral content and intermittent supply may affect taste and reliability.
column4: No publicly available data for parameters such as pH, TDS, nitrates or metals. The city’s infrastructure serves most residents, but some rural areas rely on wells or tankered water.
column5: Water is disinfected with chlorine; occasional boil‑water advisories may occur during system failures.
column6: Must meet NOM‑127‑SSA1‑1994 standards; compliance reports are not routinely published.
column7: Unknown; supply and quality may fluctuate seasonally.
column8: Potential issues include hardness, TDS, nitrates and microbial contamination. Without data, these remain speculative.
column9: Pump operation and chlorination consume energy; no advanced treatment.
column10: Limited routine monitoring for chlorine and coliforms; no microplastic or PFAS monitoring.
column11: Conventional chlorination; future improvements might include filtration or desalination.
column12: Lack of data impedes assessment; infrastructure maintenance and groundwater depletion are concerns.
column13: Implementing regular monitoring and public reporting; exploring water reuse and conservation.
